hypotheses.text: The total number of published molecularly confirmed individuals with Jaberi-Elahi syndrome worldwide remains fewer than 20 cases across fewer than 10 independent kindreds or cohorts, leading to an overestimation of 100% penetrance for hallmark neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative features.
hypotheses.rationale: Small total case numbers across the published literature (reflected in reviews analyzing small citation clusters such as Soğukpınar et al. referencing cases [4, 7-11, 14] plus sporadic inclusions in sequencing series like Bertoli-Avella or D'Abrusco) can create ascertainment bias where severe features appear invariant.

evidence.text: Soğukpınar et al. report the first Turkish case and collate all previously reported cases across the literature, citing only about seven primary publications [4, 7-11, 14] summarizing the global clinical spectrum in Table 1.

hypotheses.text: A significant fraction of GTPBP2-deficient individuals are initially misclassified as Joubert syndrome or ciliary pontocerebellar malformations due to false-positive imaging interpretation of severe cerebellar hypoplasia as a molar tooth sign (MTS).
hypotheses.rationale: D'Abrusco et al. showed that patients referred for Joubert syndrome testing because of suspected molar tooth sign harbor mutations in other brain malformation genes, specifically identifying GTPBP2/Jaberi-Elahi syndrome among the cohort.

evidence.text: In a cohort of six patients referred for Joubert syndrome testing with negative JS gene panels, exome sequencing identified pathogenic GTPBP2 variants causing Jaberi-Elahi syndrome, after expert neuroradiology review showed misrecognition of cerebellar hypoplasia as molar tooth sign.

source.title: Get your molar tooth right: Joubert syndrome misdiagnosis unmasked by whole-exome sequencing

hypotheses.text: Basal ganglia iron accumulation is an age-dependent or variable late-stage manifestation in GTPBP2 deficiency rather than an early universal hallmark, occurring in only a minority of molecularly confirmed individuals.
hypotheses.rationale: GTPBP2 has been categorized as a rare NBIA (neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation) gene in Iranian cohorts and databases, yet early infantile cases present primarily with pontocerebellar/cerebellar atrophy and optic atrophy without documented T2 hypointensity of the globus pallidus or substantia nigra.

evidence.text: GTPBP2 is described as one of the latest NBIA-associated genes identified in an Iranian kindred, falling into the heterogeneous group of hereditary neurological disorders with abnormal iron accumulation in the basal ganglia.

new_directions.question_text: What are the exact patient-by-patient clinical and neuroimaging phenotypes recorded in Table 1 of Soğukpınar et al. (2026) across all cited cases [4, 7-11, 14]?
new_directions.rationale: Soğukpınar et al. (2026) conducted a systematic aggregation of all previously reported cases into a single comparative table, which would provide definitive per-cohort numerators and denominators for optic atrophy, microcephaly, spasticity, and iron accumulation.

new_directions.question_text: In how many confirmed GTPBP2 cases has susceptibility-weighted (SWI) or T2* gradient echo MRI confirmed basal ganglia iron deposition, and at what patient age?
new_directions.rationale: Resolving whether GTPBP2 is genuinely an NBIA-spectrum disorder versus a cerebellar/neurodevelopmental disorder with secondary degenerative changes clarifies whether iron accumulation can be used as an exclusion or inclusion criterion.
